#DATAFRAME

```{r}
### Creating a data frame using the `data.frame()` function. Here we
### create a data frame with three columns named id, value, and type.
a <- data.frame(
  id = 1:5,
  value = rnorm(5),
  type = sample(LETTERS[1:2], size = 5, replace = TRUE)
)
a
typeof(a)
class(a)
attributes(a)

### We can also create data frames by converting appropriate lists.
b <- list(
  id = 1:5,
  value = rnorm(5),
  type = sample(LETTERS[1:2], size = 5, replace = TRUE)
)
b
b <- as.data.frame(b)
b

### Data frames can also be created by manually adding attributes
### to a list that meets the constraints for data frames.
b <- list(
  id = 1:5,
  value = rnorm(5),
  type = sample(LETTERS[1:2], size = 5, replace = TRUE)
)
class(b) <- "data.frame"
rownames(b) <- 1:5
b
class(b)

### Data frames are naturally created by importing data.  Here we
### import a dataset containing offers for used cars.
a <- read.csv(file = "../../sgh-r-basic-data/cars.csv", header = TRUE)
typeof(a)
class(a)

### For large data frames, printing them in their entirety is not
### particularly convenient. We have simple functions that provide an
### aggregate structure of the data frame
dim(a) # dimensions of the data frame
str(a) # more detailed structure of the data frame

### We can also look at the first few or the last few observations.
### If the number of columns exceeds the allowed width, the output
### will be wrapped onto several lines.
head(a)
tail(a)
```

```{r}
### Example of two data frames and column-wise joining.
a <- data.frame(
  id = 1:5,
  values = rnorm(5)
)
b <- data.frame(
  class = sample(LETTERS[1:2], size = 5, replace = TRUE)
)

cbind(a, b)

### Example of two data frames and row binding.
a <- data.frame(
  id = 1:5,
  values = rnorm(5),
  class = sample(LETTERS[1:2], size = 5, replace = TRUE)
)
b <- data.frame(
  id = 6:10,
  values = rnorm(5),
  class = sample(LETTERS[1:2], size = 5, replace = TRUE)
)

rbind(a, b)
```

#SUBSETTING

##Vectoer Subsetting

```{r}
### The basic method of indexing is to provide a vector of
### positions. Remember that even a single number is already a vector.
x <- 5:1 # creating a sample vector
x

x[1] # first element; indexing starts from 1, not 0
x[5] # fifth element
x[c(1, 3, 5)] # first, third, and fifth element
x[c(1, 1, 5, 5)] # repeatedly occurring elements
x[1:3] # the position vector is generated
x[3:5] # the position vector is generated
x[5:3] # the position vector is generated
x[length(x)] # always the last element of the vector
x[-1] # creating a new vector by removing an element
x[-5] # creating a new vector by removing an element
x[-(2:4)] # creating a new vector by removing multiple elements
x[1] <- 123 # changing the value of a vector at a given position
x[1:3] <- 5:7 # changing the value of a vector at multiple positions
x[1:3] <- 0 # using the recycling rule to change the values of multiple items


### Vectors can be indexed by logical vectors, which are usually the
### result of computations. A logical vector is typically the same
### length as the vector being indexed. If the value at position i is
### TRUE, that position is included in the result. If the value at
### position i is FALSE, that position is not included in the result.
y <- round(rnorm(20), 2) # Creating a sample vector
y

y[y < 0] # selecting all negative values
y[y > 0] # selecting all positive values
y[(y > 0) & (y < 1)] # selecting all values between 0 and 1
y[(y < -1) | (y > 1)] # selecting values either less than -1 or greater than 1
y[!(y < 0)] # selecting non-negative values

### Indices do not have to be created based on the vector to which
### they are applied. Below, based on the yTypes vector, which gives
### the types of observations in the y vector, we select only the
### observations for a single type.
yTypes <- sample(LETTERS[1:2], size = length(y), replace = TRUE)
yTypes

idx <- yTypes == "A"
idx
y[idx]

### Vectors can also be indexed by specifying a name. Of course, for
### this to be possible, the vector must have keys. This method is
### very rarely used.
x <- c(pierwsza = 4, druga = 3, trzecia = 1)
x

x["pierwsza"] # a single string is a vector
x[c("pierwsza", "trzecia")] # selecting multiple values
```

```{r}
### Creating data for plotting a function
n <- 3 * 10^2 # number of points
x <- seq(-2 * pi, 2 * pi, length.out = n) # x-values grid
y <- sin(x^2)/x + x # calculation of y value

### Indexing
idx <- y > 0

### Chart
plot(x, y, col = "white") # creating an "empty" plot
abline(h = 0, col = "gray") # overlaying the horizontal axis
abline(v = 0, col = "gray") # overlaying the vertical axis
abline(a = 0, b = 1, lty = "dashed", col = "blue") # adding a slanted asymptote
points(x[idx], y[idx], col = "blue", pch = 20, cex = 0.7) # points corresponding to positive values
points(x[!idx], y[!idx], col = "red", pch = 20, cex = 0.7) # points corresponding to negative values
```

```{r}
### Creating a sample
n <- 3 * 10^3 # sample size
x <- rnorm(n) # x coordinates
y <- rnorm(n) # y coordinates

### Index
idx <- x * y > 0
idxDisk <- x^2 + y^2 <= 1/2

### Creating a plot
plot(x, y, col = "white", asp = 1)
abline(h = 0, col = "gray")
abline(v = 0, col = "gray")
points(x[idx & idxDisk], y[idx & idxDisk], pch = 20, col = "steelblue3")
points(x[!idx & idxDisk], y[!idx & idxDisk], pch = 20, col = "orange3")
points(x[idx & !idxDisk], y[idx & !idxDisk], pch = 20, col = "steelblue1")
points(x[!idx & !idxDisk], y[!idx & !idxDisk], pch = 20, col = "orange1")
```

##Matrix Subsetting

```{r}
### Creating an example matrix
a <- matrix(round(rnorm(5 * 6), 2), 5, 6)
a

### Indexing by specifying position
a[1, 1]
a[2, 3]
a[c(1, 3), c(2, 3)]
a[1:2, 2:3]
a[1:2, ] # all columns
a[, 2:3] # all rows

### Indexing by specifying logical vectors 
a[a[,1] > 0, ] # all rows where the first column has a positive value
a[, a[2, ] > 0] # all columns where the second row has a positive value
a[a[,1] > 0, a[2, ] > 0] # all rows where the first
                         # column has a positive value and all
                         # columns where the second row has
                         # a positive value

### Indexing by specifying label
colnames(a) <- LETTERS[1:(dim(a)[2])]
rownames(a) <- letters[1:(dim(a)[1])]
a

a["a", "A"]
a[c("a", "c"), c("A", "D", "F")]

### Mixed indexing, different types in different dimensions.
a[c("a", "c"), 2:3]
a[a[,4] < 0, 2:3]
a[1:3, a[2, ] > 0]

### If after indexing we are left with a matrix that has only
### one row or only one column, the dim attribute is automatically "lost"
### which causes automatic conversion to
### a vector. We can prevent this by using the argument drop =
### FALSE.
a
a[, 2]
a[, 2, drop = FALSE]
```
